extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys, agents, applicants) handling U.S. design patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: MPEP guidance for examination and prosecution of U.S. design patent applications, focusing on definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first and second paragraphs), and restriction practice under 35 U.S.C. 121 for multiple embodiments/groups. Includes examiner form paragraphs, telephone restriction procedures, and required applicant responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness of claim language (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definiteness must be analyzed not in a vacuum but in light of the teachings of the prior art and of the particular application disclosure as it would be interpreted by one possessing ordinary skill in the pertinent art (In re Moore). Claims may appear indefinite when read in a vacuum but may be definite upon reading of the application disclosure or prior art teachings; conversely an otherwise definite claim in a vacuum may be uncertain when read in light of the disclosure and prior art. See MPEP § 2173.05(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of broadening phrases (e.g., 'or the like', 'or similar article') may render claims indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of phrases in the claim such as 'or similar article,' 'or the like,' or equivalent terminology has been held to be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte Pappas (23 USPQ2d 1636) is cited. However, the use of such broadening language in the title when directed to the environment of the article embodying the design should not be the basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph (see MPEP § 1503.01). Examiner form paragraphs and examiner notes provide bracketed text for inserting the objectionable phrase when preparing rejections or examiner amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation of indefinite phrase as remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Cancellation of the objectionable phrase in the claim and each occurrence of the title throughout the papers, except the oath or declaration, will overcome the rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph ¶ 15.69.01 (Remove Indefinite Language by Examiner's Amendment) is used to record cancellation by examiner after authorization (e.g., telephone interview). Bracketed placeholders in form paragraphs indicate where to insert the objectionable phrase (e.g., --or the like--).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title must identify a known article of manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is indefinite when the title fails to identify an article of manufacture and the drawing disclosure does not inherently identify the article in which the design is embodied; the drawing disclosure referenced by 'as shown' is incorporated into the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifying the title by specifying the article in which the design is embodied may introduce new matter (35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121). If the title is too ambiguous for proper examination under 37 CFR 1.104, applicant must be required to explain the nature and intended use of the article in a separate paper (not inserted into the specification). See MPEP § 1503.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information required from applicant when title is ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: When the title of the article in which the design is embodied or applied is too ambiguous and therefore indefinite, the applicant is required to provide a sufficient explanation of the nature and intended use of the article so proper classification and reliable search can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helpful additional information includes analogous fields of search, pertinent prior art, advertising brochures, and filing of copending utility applications (provide utility application number if filed). This information should be submitted as a separate paper and not inserted in the specification (37 CFR 1.56; see also 37 CFR 1.97, 1.98 and 1.99).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship and overlap between 35 U.S.C. 112 first and second paragraphs in design practice
rubrics_metrics.description: While requirements of the first and second paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 112 are separate and distinct, the relationship between them is not always easily distinguishable in design patent practice because the drawing disclosure (equivalent to written description) is incorporated into the claim by use of 'as shown.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection under both paragraphs should be made when the drawing disclosure and the claim disagree, conflict, or are inconsistent (other than in scope), and confusion exists as to whether the claimed design is sufficiently disclosed in the enabling teachings of the drawings. Example: claim directed to a chair while drawing discloses a table — reject under both paragraphs for nonenabling disclosure and indefiniteness. When amendment to drawings introduces new matter, it may give rise to a 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph rejection (35 U.S.C. 132).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first and/or second paragraphs) — use and content
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim may be rejected as not described in full, clear, concise and exact terms to enable one skilled in the art to make and use the invention (first paragraph) and/or for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention (second paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate rejections under the first and/or second paragraph are preferred; this combined paragraph should be used only when uncertainty exists as to whether the claimed invention is sufficiently described or whether the claim language is indefinite. A full explanation should be provided with such a rejection. If a design claim would otherwise be patentable but for the presence of any 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection(s), Form Paragraph 15.58.01 may be used to indicate the design is patentable over the references cited pending resolution of the 112 issue(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction practice in design applications (35 U.S.C. 121) — general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent application may only have a single claim and thus must be limited to a single invention; the examiner will require restriction in each design application which contains more than one invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restriction may be required under 35 U.S.C. 121 if subject matter disclosed in the drawings is either independent or distinct and able to support separate design patents. If embodiments are patentably indistinct and can be covered by a single claim, a rejection of one embodiment over the prior art will apply equally to other embodiments. See relevant case law (e.g., Ex parte Appeal No. 315-40).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent inventions — when restriction is proper
rubrics_metrics.description: Design inventions are independent if there is no apparent relationship between two or more disparate articles disclosed in the drawings (e.g., eyeglasses and a door handle; bicycle and camera).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restriction is clearly proper where independent inventions are present. Such situations are rare but may occur; see MPEP § 806.04 for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct inventions — difference in overall appearance or scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Design inventions are distinct if the overall appearance of two or more embodiments of an article as disclosed in the drawings are different in appearance or scope and their appearances are patentable (novel and unobvious) over each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restriction is proper where designs are patentably distinct. In determining patentable distinctness under 35 U.S.C. 121, a prior art search may be necessary. Distinct designs may be multiple embodiments of the same article or related as combination/subcombination of the overall design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple embodiments allowed only when patentably indistinct (single inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible to illustrate more than one embodiment of a design in a single application only if they involve a single inventive concept and are not patentably distinct from one another (In re Rubinfield).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure should make clear that multiple embodiments are disclosed and particularize the differences between embodiments. If one embodiment relies on another for completeness to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, the figure descriptions should identify the differences and incorporate the disclosure of the referenced embodiment. If embodiments are patentably distinct (i.e., not obvious variations), restriction must be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of the obviousness standard (35 U.S.C. 103(a)) to determine retention of multiple embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: The obviousness standard under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) must be applied in determining whether multiple embodiments may be retained in a single application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences between embodiments must either be de minimis and unrelated to their overall aesthetic appearance or be obvious to a designer of ordinary skill in view of analogous prior art in order to be retained in a single application. If embodiments are not considered obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103(a), restriction must be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction procedure — grouping, election, and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When embodiments divide into patentably distinct groups, restriction is required under 35 U.S.C. 121 to one of the identified patentably distinct groups of designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reply must include an election of a single group for prosecution on the merits even if the requirement is traversed (37 CFR 1.143). Any reply that does not include election of a single group will be held nonresponsive. Applicant is requested to cancel drawings and descriptions directed to nonelected groups. If applicant traverses on the grounds groups are not patentably distinct, applicant should present evidence then of record showing the groups to be obvious variations. If groups remain and are later determined not patentably distinct, any rejection of one group over prior art will apply equally to all other groups, and arguments based on differences will not be considered after grouping determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious variations within a group — grouping strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Embodiments disclosed within each group may be considered obvious variations of one another within the group; such embodiments comprise a single inventive concept and are grouped together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restriction is still required between patentably distinct groups, but embodiments within a group that are obvious variations need not be restricted from each other. Examiner notes provide bracketed group/embodiment placeholders and require explanation of differences between groups where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone restriction procedures and provisional election/affirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Telephone discussions between examiner and applicant may result in provisional elections or telephone restrictions; affirmation of provisional election should be made by applicant in replying to the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs ¶ 15.28, ¶ 15.28.01, ¶ 15.30 and related telephone restriction entries provide templates: indicate provisional election, record the telephone provisional election details (who, date), specify whether the provisional election was with or without traverse, and note that a group may be withdrawn by the examiner (37 CFR 1.142(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination/subcombination (difference in scope) — when separate protection is required
rubrics_metrics.description: A design claim covers the entire design as a whole, but may cover embodiments of different scope (combination vs subcombination/element) within a single application only if the designs are not patentably distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If embodiments directed to combinations vs subcombinations are patentably distinct, the designs are considered separate inventions requiring separate claims. Design protection does not extend to patentably distinct segregable parts; separate patents are needed to protect segregable parts. Case law: In re Rubinfield; Blumcraft v. Ladd; In re Kelly; Ex parte Sanford; Ex parte Heckman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction for segregable parts or combination/subcombination
rubrics_metrics.description: When disclosed embodiments relate to segregable parts or distinct combinations/subcombinations, restriction to one of the inventions is required under 35 U.S.C. 121.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grouped inventions are distinct because a design patent covers only the invention disclosed as an entirety and does not extend to patentably distinct segregable parts; applicant must elect a group and cancel figures directed to nonelected groups. Action on the merits is deferred pending compliance (Ex parte Heckman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional election requirement (37 CFR 1.143)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant is advised that the reply to be complete must include a provisional election of one of the enumerated designs, even though the requirement may be traversed (37 CFR 1.143).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to include a provisional election in the reply will render the reply incomplete/nonresponsive. Telephone provisional elections must later be affirmed in the written reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner notes and use of form paragraphs in design prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of specific form paragraphs and examiner notes to implement rejections, amendments, restriction requirements, telephone restrictions, and cancellation of objectionable language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP provides bracketed form paragraph templates (e.g., ¶ 15.22.02, ¶ 15.69.01, ¶ 15.27 through ¶ 15.31, ¶ 15.58.01) with examiner notes indicating where to insert embodiments, groups, objectionable phrases, and explanations. Examiners should follow these templates and fill bracketed items; the notes explain when to use combined 112 rejections or separate ones and how to instruct applicants regarding elections and cancellations.
